body.text: Donald Trump was inaugurated for his second term as U.S. president on January 20, 2025. Since then, his administration has imposed sweeping tariffs on virtually every country in Southeast Asia. These were later knocked down by the Supreme Court, but not before Indonesia and Malaysia cut rather lopsided bilateral deals. The administration also oversaw the dismantling of USAID, which had maintained a significant presence in many Southeast Asian countries for decades.

Under Trump 2.0 the United States withdrew from the Just Energy Transition Partnerships it helped launch in Vietnam and Indonesia. And it continues to practice an erratic trade policy across the region, re-imposing tariffs on some countries and industries in pursuit of ambiguous goals. The administration seems particularly eager to clamp down on countries it believes are acting as transshipment points for Chinese goods looking to evade U.S. tariffs.

The U.S. conflict with Iran has driven energy prices higher, putting real economic and fiscal pressure on governments, consumers, and businesses across the region. The Philippines, a long-time U.S. ally, is being squeezed especially hard here as it is heavily exposed to energy imports. Taken together, U.S. economic engagement in the region over the last two years has been highly volatile, disruptive, and subject to unpredictable whims.

The Democrats surged to big majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate during the mid-term elections and many are interpreting this as a rebuke of Trump’s second term policies and style of governance. Does this mean in the final two years of his term we will see a milder and more constrained Donald Trump who works together with Democrats and foreign partners as collaborators, rather than the unpredictable and adversarial Trump we have come to expect?

I think that would be extremely unlikely. When it comes to how the United States does business in Southeast Asia and pursues investment and trade deals, we should expect more of the same: erratic policies, ambiguous goals, and blunt methods. While the Democrats have snatched a huge majority in the House and flipped the Senate, they lack the votes to credibly threaten Trump with impeachment or to override a presidential veto. There’s a limit to what they can do, and even then much of their attention will be focused on domestic issues.

What they can do is launch investigations and squeeze federal funding and appropriations, but such efforts will likely focus on defunding conflict in Iran and domestic issues such as immigration and corruption. Despite the landslide victory for Democrats, the president retains considerable authority when it comes to trade and foreign policy, and a Democrat-controlled Congress is unlikely to spend its political capital pushing the Trump administration to become a more rational economic actor in Southeast Asia. The “blue tsunami” will do little to stop Trump from arbitrarily threatening countries with tariffs.

One area where the dynamic might shift significantly is AI supply chains. Southeast Asia has been riding a big wave of investment, including from the United States, in data centers and the production and trade of critical minerals, semiconductors, and computer chips. Now Singapore-based cloud computing and AI infrastructure firm Megaspeed has emerged at the center of a major scandal involving infidelity, national security, and U.S. chip-making giant Nvidia.

The allegation is that Nvidia was selling advanced computer chips to Megaspeed, which then routed or provided remote access to Chinese firms in order to evade U.S. export controls. Until now, the United States has not been that interested in looking deeply at the AI supply chains spanning Southeast Asia. That is likely to change over the next two years, with increased Congressional scrutiny of AI supply chains, the role played by Southeast Asia, and whether the Trump administration was too lax in monitoring them.

A Democrat-controlled Congress is not likely to interfere much in how the Trump administration conducts economic policy in Southeast Asia, and we should not expect huge changes from how Trump has conducted policy in the past. The United States will continue to engage with Southeast Asia using an unpredictable mix of threats and tariffs, while the national security aspect of chip exports and AI supply chains will undoubtedly become a more prominent issue in the next two years.

But for the most part, Trump’s final two years in office, even with big Democrat majorities in Congress, will almost certainly be more of the same. The damage inflicted during the first two years has already been done and will be hard to roll back. Anyone hoping that a wipeout during the mid-terms would radically change the terms of trade and investment or lead to a softer Trump and more predictable trade and economic policies is likely to be disappointed.
